questions.title: How do iterative and recursive Fibonacci solutions work in Go
questions.direct_answer: The Fibonacci sequence starts with zero and one, and each later value is the sum of the previous two. A function must state whether `F(0)=0` and `F(1)=1` before calculating later terms. An iterative solution carries only the previous two values through a loop. The direct recursive definition calls `fib(n-1)` and `fib(n-2)`, so it repeats the same subproblems many times.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The Fibonacci sequence starts with zero and one, and each later value is the sum of the previous two. A function must state whether `F(0)=0` and `F(1)=1` before calculating later terms.

An iterative solution carries only the previous two values through a loop. The direct recursive definition calls `fib(n-1)` and `fib(n-2)`, so it repeats the same subproblems many times.

For example, starting with `a=0` and `b=1`, three updates produce pairs `(1,1)`, `(1,2)`, and `(2,3)`, so `F(4)` is `3` under the zero-based definition.

A machine integer eventually overflows even when the algorithm is correct. Negative indexes need rejection or an explicitly defined extension, and huge exact values need `math/big.Int`.

Choose iteration for a single non-negative index when you want simple code, linear time, and constant extra space. It also avoids growing the call stack.

sections.content:

The recurrence describes the relationship between values, but it does not force a recursive implementation. A loop computes the same dependency chain from the known base cases upward. Tracking the pair before every update gives a useful invariant: `a` is the current Fibonacci value and `b` is the next one.

sections.title: Why the failure happens: Fibonacci in Go
sections.content:
Failures around Fibonacci in Go usually come from one incorrect assumption about ownership, state, ordering, or lifetime. Finding that assumption is more useful than adding a defensive line at random.

The recursive call graph branches twice at most non-base nodes. Many branches request the same indexes, so the number of calls grows roughly like the sequence itself. A cache changes that behaviour because the first result for each index is reused; bottom-up iteration avoids the calls entirely.

Fibonacci in Go and the recursive definition solve related problems, but they expose different guarantees. The best choice follows from the guarantee the program actually needs.
